name: Otjize (Himba red ochre skin paste)

image.caption: Himba woman applying otjize to her body in northern Namibia, 2007

lead: Otjize is a paste of butterfat and red ochre pigment used by the Himba people of Namibia. It gives skin and hair a distinctive red colour and is part of Himba beauty and cultural practice.
It is also used for protection from sun and insects. A 2022 laboratory study of the Namibian ochre found strong UV filtration and infrared reflectivity.

paras: Himba women and, historically, men apply the paste to skin and to plaited hair, sometimes scented with aromatic resin from Commiphora multijuga.
No clinical safety trials of otjize are published. The laboratory study examined the ochre's physical properties, not application on people.

angle.text: The paste is used as both adornment and sun protection. Laboratory results show UV filtration by the ochre itself.

lead: Otjize is a paste made from butterfat and ochre, a red clay pigment, used by the Himba people of Namibia. It is often perfumed with the resin of Commiphora multijuga, called omuzumba, and applied to both skin and hair.[1]

It serves several purposes at once: protection from the desert sun and climate, insect repellence, hair styling, hygiene where water is scarce, and ceremonial roles including initiation and burial.[1] Women begin styling their hair at puberty. Men's use declined from the 1960s.[1]

In 2022, researchers published a Scientific Reports study of the natural Namibian red ochre, reporting nanoscale hematite crystals with strong UV filtration and infrared reflectivity, plus antibacterial activity against E. coli and S. aureus in vitro.[2] The authors linked this to the Himba community's reported low skin cancer rate.[2]
infobox: Butterfat, red ochre, sometimes aromatic resin

paras: The paste is applied to skin and long, plaited hair, and gradually flakes off, which the Wikipedia article describes as a way of removing dirt and dead skin.[1] It is also documented as a mosquito repellent.[1]
Otjize marks initiation and burial and has become a symbol in literature: Nnedi Okorafor's Hugo Award-winning novella Binti (2015) features it as a sign of home and cultural identity.[1]

No studies found in people. A 2022 materials study characterised the red ochre as alpha-Fe2O3 nanocrystals with strong UV filtration and infrared reflectivity, and reported antibacterial activity in vitro.[2]
